title: Getting Hired as an ED Tech
summary: What the job is called, what hospitals require, how to write a resume and answer the interview, and how to use the first ninety days to become the tech everyone wants and the applicant PA schools want.

lessons.title: One job, many names, three kinds of building
lessons.body:
## The same job posted six ways

If you search one title you will miss most of the openings. The same role is posted as:

- Emergency department technician, or ED tech
- ER technician
- Patient care technician - emergency, often written PCT-ED
- Clinical technician, clinical associate, or clinical care partner
- Emergency care technician (ECT)
- Nursing assistant - emergency, at systems that built the job off the nursing assistant ladder

Some systems also post **paramedic - ED**. That is a different, higher-paid job with a wider scope. Apply to it only if you hold a paramedic certification.

> **Key:** Search every title, plus the words "emergency" and "technician" separately. The job you want may be posted as "Patient Care Technician II - Emergency Services" and never use the word "tech" at all.

## Three kinds of emergency department

The building changes the job more than the title does.

An **academic Level I trauma center** takes the worst trauma in its region, has residents and fellows learning on the floor, and has a written protocol for almost everything. You see more, you personally do fewer procedures because residents want them, and you work inside heavy structure. The teaching culture helps if you are heading to PA school, because everyone around you is already in the habit of explaining.

A **community ED** sees roughly 100 to 250 patients a day, staffs attending physicians and PAs but usually no residents, and runs on a small permanent crew. Techs there own more: blood draws, EKGs, splints, catheters, sometimes IVs. You get hands on things sooner and you get known faster.

A **freestanding ED**, a satellite emergency department with no hospital attached to it, stabilizes and then transfers or discharges. One or two techs, so you do everything. The average acuity is lower, but a heart attack still walks through that door and you still run it.

## The map around Camden County

Postings turn over weekly. This is a map of where to look, not a claim that any of these is hiring today.

| System | Where | Flavor |
|---|---|---|
| Cooper University Health Care | Camden | Academic; the only Level I trauma center in South Jersey |
| Virtua Health | Voorhees, Marlton, Camden, Mount Holly | The largest community system in South Jersey |
| Jefferson Health New Jersey | Cherry Hill, Stratford, Washington Township | Community EDs with an academic parent |
| Inspira Health | Mullica Hill, Vineland, Woodbury, Elmer | Gloucester and Cumberland counties |
| AtlantiCare | Atlantic City, Pomona | Shore region, high summer volume |
| Penn Medicine | Philadelphia | Academic |
| Temple University Hospital | North Philadelphia | Level I, very high penetrating trauma volume |
| ChristianaCare | Newark, Delaware | Level I, one of the busiest EDs in the country |

Applying across the bridge is normal. Philadelphia systems hire New Jersey residents constantly. Weigh the commute against what a 45-minute drive feels like at 7:30 in the morning after a night shift.

## The one question that tells you the truth

Scope varies by department, not by title. One hospital's tech draws blood and starts peripheral IVs; the hospital four miles away does not let techs touch a needle at all.

> **On shift:** Ask it plainly in the interview: "What does the tech actually do here?" The answer tells you whether this job builds the skills you want, and asking it marks you as someone who thinks about the work instead of the paycheck.
keyPoints: Search at least six title variants; many postings never use the word 'tech'.
Academic Level I centers give structure, teaching, and a resume line; community EDs give hands and autonomy sooner.
A freestanding ED has no inpatient beds, so it stabilizes and then transfers or discharges.
Tech scope is set by the department, not the title, so ask what techs actually do there.
Cooper in Camden is the only Level I trauma center in South Jersey.

checks.q: You search a hospital career site for 'ED tech' and find nothing. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The hospital does not employ technicians
The role is posted under a different title such as 'Patient Care Technician - Emergency'
Only internal employees can see technician postings
Technician jobs are posted only in the spring
checks.why: Systems use different names for the same job: PCT-ED, clinical associate, emergency care technician. Searching one phrase hides most of the market. Internal-only postings exist but are far less common than a naming mismatch.

checks.q: What is the main practical difference between a freestanding ED and a hospital-based ED?
choices: The freestanding ED only treats minor complaints by law
The freestanding ED has no inpatient beds, so sick patients are stabilized and transferred
The freestanding ED does not have to follow EMTALA
The freestanding ED cannot perform EKGs or labs
checks.why: A freestanding ED is a full emergency department without a hospital attached; anyone needing admission gets transferred. It is still bound by EMTALA, still runs labs and EKGs, and cannot refuse a critically ill patient who walks in.

checks.q: Why does asking 'what does the tech actually do here' matter more than reading the job description?
choices: Job descriptions are legally meaningless
Scope is set department by department, so two hospitals with identical postings can have very different tech roles
It is the only way to learn the pay range
Managers are required to answer it truthfully
checks.why: Postings are written by HR and recycled for years. Whether techs draw blood, start IVs, or splint is a local decision made by the ED's leadership, and it determines what skills the job will build.

lessons.title: What they require and how to get each one
lessons.body:
## The list is shorter than it looks

Most ED tech postings in New Jersey ask for four things you control and four things the hospital does to you after the offer.

| Requirement | What counts | Time to get | Approximate cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| High school diploma or GED | Transcript or diploma copy | Have it | None |
| EMT certification | New Jersey OEMS certification, obtained by passing the National Registry cognitive exam plus the state-approved psychomotor (skills) exam | 3 to 6 months of course | About `$1,000` to `$1,500`, less through a county or volunteer squad program |
| BLS Provider | American Heart Association **BLS Provider** card, or American Red Cross BLS; valid 2 years | 1 day | About `$60` to `$100` |
| Phlebotomy certificate | Often "preferred," occasionally required | 4 to 10 week course | `$800` to `$2,000` plus about `$125` exam |
| EKG certificate | Almost always "preferred," usually trained on the job | 4 to 8 weeks | `$500` to `$1,200` plus about `$120` exam |

> **Trap:** An online-only CPR card with no hands-on skills check will be rejected at employee health. Hospitals want AHA BLS Provider (blended HeartCode is fine as long as you completed the in-person skills session), not a layperson "CPR certified" certificate.

## The certifications that move you up the pile

New Jersey does not license phlebotomists, so a certificate is legally optional. It still matters, because it tells a manager she does not have to teach you to draw blood and it often bumps your starting step. The common credential is the National Healthcareer Association **CPT**. NHA requires evidence of at least 30 successful venipunctures and 10 capillary or finger sticks on live individuals before you can sit for it.

The EKG equivalent is the NHA **CET**. Most departments will teach you a 12-lead in a week, so this one is a tiebreaker rather than a requirement.

## The four things that happen after the offer

Every offer is contingent. Failing any of these cancels it.

**Background check.** Criminal history, sometimes fingerprinting, plus verification of every job and school you listed. Discrepancies in dates are a bigger problem than most people expect. List real months.

**Drug screen.** Usually a 10-panel urine test within 24 to 72 hours of the offer. New Jersey law limits what employers may do based on a cannabis test alone, but hospitals holding federal contracts and safety-sensitive employers still test and still rescind offers. Do not treat legalization as protection for a pre-employment screen.

**Immunizations and titers.** Expect proof of MMR (two doses or a positive titer), varicella, a Tdap dose (healthcare personnel get one Tdap regardless of interval, then a Td or Tdap booster every 10 years), hepatitis B series plus a surface antibody titer, annual influenza during the season, and COVID per current policy. The hepatitis B series is the long pole: doses at `0`, `1`, and `6` months, then a titer 1 to 2 months after the last dose. Start it the day you decide you want this job.

**TB screening and fit test.** Either a two-step tuberculin skin test, which means four visits over 1 to 3 weeks, or a single IGRA blood test such as QuantiFERON, which is one visit. Then an N95 respirator fit test, required annually under OSHA, about 20 minutes at employee health.

> **Key:** Nothing on this list is hard. All of it is slow. The applicant who started the hepatitis B series and the EMT course three months early is the one who can start in two weeks instead of five.
keyPoints: New Jersey EMT certification comes through NJ OEMS after passing the National Registry cognitive exam and the state-approved psychomotor exam; the National Registry no longer administers the EMT psychomotor exam.
The card hospitals want is AHA BLS Provider, valid 2 years, not a layperson CPR certificate.
Phlebotomy (NHA CPT) and EKG (NHA CET) certificates are usually 'preferred' and can raise your starting step.
Hepatitis B is a 0, 1, and 6 month series plus a titer, so it takes 7 to 8 months and should be started early.
A two-step TB skin test needs four visits; a single IGRA blood test needs one.

checks.q: A posting says 'BLS required.' Which card satisfies it?
choices: An online CPR course completion certificate
AHA BLS Provider, including the in-person skills check
A first aid certificate from a community class
Any CPR card less than five years old
checks.why: Hospitals require a healthcare-provider level BLS card with a hands-on skills evaluation, valid 2 years. Online-only cards, lay first aid cards, and expired or five-year cards are rejected at employee health.

checks.q: Why should you start the hepatitis B vaccine series before you even apply?
choices: It is required before you can sit for the NREMT
The series is given at 0, 1, and 6 months plus a titer afterward, so it can delay a start date by months
Hospitals will not interview unvaccinated applicants
The titer expires after 90 days
checks.why: The three-dose series plus the post-series surface antibody titer takes 7 to 8 months. It is not required to test for the NREMT and does not block an interview, but an incomplete series is the most common reason a start date slides.

checks.q: A posting lists 'phlebotomy certification preferred.' You do not have one. What is the correct move?
choices: Do not apply until you are certified
Apply now, and say honestly that you are enrolled or willing to certify
List it on the resume and get it before orientation
Ask HR to waive the requirement in writing
checks.why: 'Preferred' is not 'required' and screening out yourself is the most common self-inflicted wound in a job search. Listing a credential you do not hold is falsification and ends the application when verification fails.

lessons.title: Reading the posting like a contract
lessons.body:
## Status: what you are actually being offered

The three words at the top of the posting decide your income, your benefits, and your life.

**Full-time** is usually written as an FTE number. `1.0` FTE is 40 hours a week, or 36 hours at hospitals that build the schedule out of twelve-hour shifts. `0.9` is 36 hours, `0.6` is 24, `0.5` is 20.

**Part-time** is anything below full. Benefits eligibility usually starts around `0.5` to `0.6` FTE, or 20 hours a week, but the threshold is set by the system, so read it.

**Per diem** (also called PRN or casual) means no benefits, a higher base rate to compensate, and a minimum commitment written into the posting, commonly two shifts a month plus one holiday a year. Per diem is excellent as a second job and a bad first job, because you get the fewest training hours and the least protection.

## Shifts and the words around them

Most EDs run twelve-hour shifts, typically `0700` to `1900` and `1900` to `0700`, with some eight- and ten-hour shifts in fast track. Three twelves is a 36-hour week.

"Every other weekend" is standard and non-negotiable almost everywhere. "Holiday rotation" means roughly half the holidays a year. "Rotating shifts" means you flip between days and nights on a cycle, which is the hardest schedule on the human body. A fixed night line is usually easier than rotating.

**Self-scheduling** means you request your own shifts inside rules (so many weekends, so many nights) before the schedule is built. **Block scheduling** means a fixed repeating pattern. Self-scheduling is worth real money in quality of life.

## Differentials: the money hiding under the base rate

| Differential | Typical add-on | When |
|---|---|---|
| Evening | `$1.50` to `$3.00` per hour | Roughly 1500 to 2300 |
| Night | `$2.00` to `$5.00` per hour | Roughly 2300 to 0700, or the whole night shift |
| Weekend | `$1.50` to `$4.00` per hour | Friday night through Sunday night, varies |
| Charge or preceptor | `$1.00` to `$2.00` per hour | When assigned |

Those ranges are approximate and vary by system. What matters is that they stack. A base rate that looks unimpressive on a posting can be three to six dollars an hour higher on the shifts you would actually work.

> **Key:** Compare jobs on the rate for the shift you will really work, not the posted base. Nights plus weekends can be a 20 to 30 percent difference on the same base rate.

## Union or not

New Jersey hospital workers are often represented, most commonly by HPAE (Health Professionals and Allied Employees) or JNESO. If the posting says "union position," expect a published step scale where pay is set by years of service, a defined probationary period, seniority rules for shift bids and time off, and dues taken from your check.

A step scale means your hourly rate is barely negotiable, but the step you start on sometimes is. Non-union means more room to negotiate and less protection.

> **Trap:** "Preferred" is not "required," and "1 year of patient care experience" is routinely waived for a certified EMT. Reading yourself out of a posting is the cheapest mistake you can make and the most common. Apply anyway.

Two more phrases to notice. A **sign-on bonus** almost always carries a payback clause if you leave inside 12 or 24 months. A **float requirement** means you can be sent to other units when the ED is overstaffed, which is either a broadening experience or an annoyance depending on the day.
keyPoints: FTE is the real status number: 1.0 is full-time, benefits usually start near 0.5 to 0.6 FTE or 20 hours a week.
Per diem pays a higher base with no benefits and a written minimum commitment, and gives the least training.
Differentials stack: evening, night, weekend, and preceptor pay can add several dollars an hour to the same base.
Union postings mean a published step scale, seniority rules, and dues, with little room to negotiate the rate.
'Preferred' qualifications and experience minimums are frequently waived for a certified EMT, so apply anyway.

checks.q: A posting reads '0.6 FTE, nights, every other weekend.' How many hours per week is that?
choices: About 12 hours
About 24 hours
About 30 hours
About 36 hours
checks.why: FTE is a fraction of full time. 0.6 of a 40-hour week is 24 hours, typically two twelve-hour shifts. 0.9 would be 36 hours and 1.0 would be full time.

checks.q: Which is the strongest argument against taking a per diem position as your first hospital job?
choices: Per diem pays less per hour
Per diem staff cannot be certified as EMTs
Per diem staff get the fewest orientation and precepted hours, which is exactly what a new tech needs most
Per diem positions never convert to full-time
checks.why: Per diem usually pays a higher base precisely because it carries no benefits, and it often does convert. The real cost is training: a new tech needs weeks of precepted shifts, and per diem schedules rarely provide them.

checks.q: Two offers have the same $21.00 base. Offer A is days; offer B is nights with a $4.00 night differential and a $2.50 weekend differential, working every other weekend. What should you compare?
choices: The base rates, since they are identical
The effective rate on the shifts you will actually work, which is materially higher for B
The sign-on bonus only
Nothing, differentials are not guaranteed income
checks.why: Differentials are paid automatically for the hours worked and stack with each other. Comparing posted base rates hides a difference that can be 20 to 30 percent of your paycheck.

lessons.title: The resume that survives the filter
lessons.body:
## Two readers, in this order

Your resume is read first by software and second by a tired manager for about 15 seconds. Both readers have rules, and the software's rules are stricter.

Hospital systems run applicant tracking software such as Workday, iCIMS, or Taleo. It converts your document into plain text and matches it against the posting. Anything that confuses the parser gets dropped silently, and you never find out.

**Rules that keep the parser happy:**

- One page, one column, no tables, no text boxes, no columns, no graphics, no photo
- Nothing important in a header or footer, because many parsers discard those regions
- Standard section names: Certifications, Experience, Education, Skills
- A common font at 10 to 12 point; save as `.docx` unless the portal asks for PDF
- File name `Lastname_Firstname_EDTech.docx`
- Reverse chronological, with month and year for every job
- Mirror the posting's exact words. If it says "point-of-care testing," write point-of-care testing, not "bedside lab tests"

> **Trap:** The beautiful two-column template with the skill bars is the single most common reason a qualified applicant is never seen. It parses into nonsense.

## What goes where

Put **Certifications** at the top, above Experience, with expiration dates: `NJ EMT-B, cert #, exp 03/2029`. That is the line the screener is looking for, so do not bury it on page one's bottom edge.

No objective statement. "Seeking a challenging position where I can grow" tells a manager nothing and burns your best real estate. Either open with two lines of specific summary or open with Certifications.

No "references available upon request." It is assumed, and it wastes a line.

## Translating service work into clinical language

Retail, food service, and call center work is not filler. It is the closest thing most first-time applicants have to the ED, because the ED is a customer-facing operation where people arrive frightened and angry. Translate honestly, do not inflate.

| What you did | How it reads on a hospital resume |
|---|---|
| Calmed down angry customers | De-escalated 20 or more confrontations per week without security involvement |
| Ran the floor during a rush | Managed 6 concurrent priorities during peak volume with no service failures |
| Trained new hires | Trained and onboarded 14 new employees; wrote the shift checklist still in use |
| Fixed a bad customer experience | Service recovery: resolved complaints at the point of contact, 2 manager escalations per month |
| Stocked and counted inventory | Maintained stock levels and par counts across 40 SKUs; zero stockouts in Q3 |
| Opened or closed, handled cash | Accountable for opening and closing procedures and cash reconciliation, audited monthly |

Stocking par levels, de-escalating an angry stranger, keeping six things straight at once, and training the new person are literally four of an ED tech's daily tasks. Say them in the hospital's vocabulary and the manager sees a colleague instead of a career changer.

> **Key:** Every bullet gets a number. "Handled customer complaints" is invisible. "Resolved 20 to 30 escalated complaints weekly" is a person who has done something.

The bullet formula is action verb, what you did, the scale, the result. Past jobs in past tense, current job in present tense. Never claim a clinical skill you have not been signed off on; verification is routine and a false claim ends the application permanently.

## The cover letter

Write one only when the portal gives you a field. Four short paragraphs: the specific role and requisition number, why emergency medicine specifically, two concrete things from your history that transfer, and one sentence on availability. Name the department. Generic letters read as spam because they are.
keyPoints: Applicant tracking software parses plain text, so one column, no tables, no graphics, nothing in headers or footers.
Certifications go at the top with expiration dates; no objective statement, no 'references upon request'.
Mirror the posting's exact vocabulary so keyword matching finds you.
Translate service work into hospital language honestly, and put a number on every bullet.
Never list a clinical skill you have not been signed off on; verification is routine.

checks.q: Why is a two-column resume template with graphics a bad choice for a hospital application?
choices: Hospitals consider it unprofessional
Applicant tracking software parses it into scrambled text and may drop content entirely
It cannot be printed by HR
It exceeds the portal file size limit
checks.why: The problem is machine, not taste. Parsers read left to right across columns and discard text boxes and header regions, so content vanishes silently before any human sees it.

checks.q: Which bullet is strongest on an ED tech resume?
choices: Responsible for customer service and problem solving
Excellent communicator with a passion for helping people
De-escalated 20 or more customer confrontations per week without security involvement
Duties included handling complaints as assigned
checks.why: It names a specific action, gives scale, and states an outcome that maps directly to ED work. The others are adjectives and job-description language, which every applicant has and no manager believes.

checks.q: Where do certifications belong on a first hospital resume?
choices: At the top, above experience, with expiration dates
At the bottom, after education
Only in the cover letter
In a sidebar next to your photo
checks.why: The screener is checking one thing first: do you hold EMT and BLS. Putting it at the top answers the gating question in the first two seconds. A sidebar also breaks the parser.

lessons.title: From application to offer, and leaving the old job well
lessons.body:
## The sequence

1. **Apply on the hospital's own career portal.** Job boards mostly repost and route you back anyway; applying at the source keeps your record clean and gets you the requisition number. Build one profile per system and save the login.
2. **Apply within 72 hours of the posting date.** Many requisitions are reviewed in batches and close early when enough applicants arrive.
3. **Recruiter phone screen, 10 to 20 minutes.** Availability, certifications, pay expectation, why the ED. Have your calendar and a pay range ready before you pick up.
4. **The panel interview, 30 to 60 minutes.** Usually the ED manager or clinical director plus a charge nurse, sometimes an educator or a senior tech. Mostly behavioral questions.
5. **Shadow shift at some departments,** 2 to 4 hours, usually unpaid, observation only with no patient contact. It is still an interview.
6. **Verbal offer, then a written offer** contingent on background check, drug screen, employee health clearance, and certification verification.
7. **Employee health visit:** immunization records, TB screening, N95 fit test.
8. **Start date,** typically 2 to 6 weeks after the offer. Application to first day usually runs `4` to `8` weeks.

> **On shift:** The shadow shift is graded even though nobody says so. Stay out of the doorway, keep your hands off everything, ask your questions in the lulls and not during a critical patient, and learn three people's names. Managers ask the staff afterward.

## Following up without becoming a problem

Send a thank-you email within 24 hours to every interviewer, three to five sentences, naming one specific thing from the conversation. It is rare enough that it is remembered.

Then follow up once, three days after whatever timeline they gave you. Then stop. A second nudge reads as anxiety and does not move a requisition.

Silence is normal and usually structural, not personal: internal candidates and union members frequently have bidding rights that must be exhausted before external applicants are considered. The automated "no longer under consideration" email is generated by software and means nothing about you personally. Reapply to the same system for a different posting; it is expected.

## The offer conversation

Ask for the offer in writing before you resign anything. Confirm in the written offer: title, FTE, base rate, shift, differentials, start date, orientation length, benefits start date, and any sign-on bonus payback clause.

Do not resign your current job on a verbal offer. Verbal offers die at drug screens and background checks.

> **Key:** Nothing is real until the offer letter is in your hand and the contingencies are cleared. Give notice after that, never before.

## Leaving a retail or service job well

The manager of a store you leave in 2026 is a reference you will need in 2029 when a PA program asks about your work history, and hospitals verify employment dates for every job you list.

- Give two weeks in writing, more if you supervise people or hold keys
- Tell your manager before you tell any coworker, without exception
- Work the schedule you already committed to, including the bad shifts
- Write down your manager's personal email and cell number before your last day, because managers move
- In the exit interview, be boring and positive. There is nothing to win there and a reference to lose
- Ask directly: "Would you be comfortable being a reference for me?" and get a yes on the record
keyPoints: Apply on the hospital's own portal within 72 hours of the posting, and keep the requisition number.
Expect recruiter screen, panel interview, possible shadow shift, contingent offer, employee health, then start.
Application to first day is typically 4 to 8 weeks.
Thank-you email within 24 hours, one follow-up after the stated timeline, then stop.
Never resign on a verbal offer, and leave the old job with the manager's personal contact and a yes on being a reference.

checks.q: You get an enthusiastic verbal offer on Tuesday. When should you give notice at your current job?
choices: Immediately, to show commitment
After the written offer arrives and the contingencies such as drug screen and background check are cleared
After your first day of orientation
Two weeks before the anticipated start date regardless of paperwork
checks.why: Offers are contingent by default and do fail at screening or verification. Resigning on a verbal offer risks having no job at all. Waiting until after orientation is too late to give proper notice.

checks.q: Two weeks after a strong interview you have heard nothing. What is the most likely reason?
choices: You were rejected and they are avoiding telling you
Internal or union candidates have bidding rights that must be exhausted first, and hospital hiring is simply slow
The posting was fraudulent
Your references gave a poor report
checks.why: Hospital requisitions routinely take weeks and often must clear internal posting or contractual bidding periods before external candidates are considered. Silence at two weeks is normal and carries no information.

checks.q: During a shadow shift, what is the correct behavior?
choices: Help with vitals to show initiative
Observe only, stay out of the way, keep hands off patients and equipment, and ask questions during lulls
Interview the staff about pay and management
Stay silent the entire time and speak to no one
checks.why: You are not credentialed, oriented, or covered, so any patient contact is a real liability problem. Staff feedback is part of the hiring decision, so total silence wastes the visit; ask good questions at the right moments.

lessons.title: The interview: STAR and the questions they ask
lessons.body:
## Why they ask about your past

Behavioral interviewing rests on one assumption: what you did before predicts what you will do here. So panels ask "tell me about a time you handled an angry person," not "how would you handle one."

**STAR** is the structure that keeps the answer under 90 seconds.

- **Situation**, one sentence. Where, when, what was happening.
- **Task**, one sentence. What was on you specifically.
- **Action**, three or four sentences. What *you* did, step by step. Say "I," not "we."
- **Result**, one sentence with a number or a concrete outcome.

> **Key:** Prepare six stories, not twenty-five answers. Six good stories cover almost every behavioral question asked, because interviewers re-slice the same material.

The six: an angry person you calmed; a mistake you made and fixed; someone you taught; a time everything happened at once and you had to prioritize; a disagreement with a supervisor; a time you did more than the job required.

## The questions that carry the most weight

**"Tell me about yourself."** Ninety seconds, three beats: where you are now and what you hold, why emergency medicine specifically, what you want to be doing in a few years. Not a biography.

**"Why the ED?"** Answer about the work, not about yourself. Undifferentiated patients, worst-first reasoning, the pace, and the fact that the tech is the hands on almost every early task. "I like helping people" is the answer everyone gives.

**"Tell me about a time you handled an angry customer."** Show listening, not winning. The result should be that the person calmed down, not that you were proven right.

**"Tell me about a mistake you made."** Pick a real one with small stakes. Own it flatly, then spend most of the answer on what you did immediately, who you told, and what you changed so it could not recur. Refusing to name one is the actual failure.

**"How do you prioritize when everything is due at once?"** Give a rule, not a feeling: life threats first, then time-critical orders such as an EKG inside 10 minutes for chest pain or sepsis labs, then everything else in order of who is waiting longest. Then add the sentence that wins the question: "and I tell the nurse out loud what I am not going to get to."

**"What if a nurse asked you to do something outside your scope?"** Three parts, in this order: decline the task, keep the relationship, solve her problem. "I'd tell her I'm not signed off on that, ask what she needs to happen, offer what I can do, and go find someone who can do the rest."

**"What is your availability?"** Say it plainly. Every hedge costs you. If you can work nights and weekends, lead with it, because that is what they are actually hiring for.

**"What is your biggest weakness?"** A real one plus the system you use to contain it. "I move fast and I used to skip writing things down, so now I carry a brain sheet and chart the time as I go."

## The other seventeen

Prepare a sentence or two for each, then map it to one of your six stories.

- Why this hospital, and why this department
- What does an ED tech do all day
- A time you worked with a difficult coworker
- A time you received criticism
- A time you had to learn something fast
- Being corrected in front of other people
- What would your last supervisor say about you
- A rule you disagreed with but followed
- How do you handle seeing something upsetting
- What do you do when you are not sure what to do
- Teamwork under pressure
- How do you keep patient information private
- A time you were bored and what you did
- What do you do in the last hour of a slow shift
- Where do you see yourself in five years
- Why are you leaving your current job
- What questions do you have for us

> **Trap:** An honest PA-school answer to "where do you see yourself in five years" is fine and often helps, paired with a commitment to this job now. What sinks candidates is making the ED sound like a waiting room.

On pay: if asked first, give a range and redirect. "From what I've seen, this role in this area runs roughly `$20` to `$25` an hour depending on certification. I'm in that range, and I care more about the schedule and the training."
keyPoints: STAR keeps an answer to 90 seconds: one sentence situation, one sentence task, three or four sentences of action, one sentence result with a number.
Prepare six stories rather than memorizing twenty-five answers.
The scope question has three parts: decline the task, keep the relationship, solve the nurse's problem.
Prioritization answers need a stated rule plus telling the nurse what you will not get to.
Answer pay questions with a range and a redirect to schedule and training.

checks.q: In a STAR answer, which part should take the most time?
choices: Situation, so the panel understands the context fully
Task, so they know it was your responsibility
Action, because it is the only part that shows what you personally do
Result, because outcomes are what matter
checks.why: Situation and task are one sentence each of scene-setting and result is one sentence of payoff. The action is the evidence, and it must be in the first person, since panels are trying to hear what you specifically did.

checks.q: A nurse asks you to push an IV medication. Which interview answer is strongest?
choices: I would do it, because the nurse is responsible for the order
I would tell her that is not my job
I would tell her I am not signed off on that, ask what she needs to happen, offer what I can do, and find someone who can do the rest
I would report her to the manager immediately
checks.why: Techs do not administer medications, so doing it is out of scope no matter who asked. 'Not my job' is technically correct and relationally fatal. Jumping to a report skips solving the actual clinical problem in front of you.

checks.q: Asked to name a weakness, which answer works?
choices: I work too hard and care too much
I move fast and used to skip writing things down, so I carry a brain sheet and chart the time as I go
I do not really have one
I struggle with authority but I am working on it
checks.why: It names a real limitation and pairs it with a system that contains it, which is exactly what the question is testing. Disguised strengths and 'none' read as evasion, and admitting an authority problem describes someone unsafe in a hierarchy that runs on orders.

lessons.title: What to ask them, what to wear, what to bring
lessons.body:
## Your questions are part of the evaluation

Every panel ends with "what questions do you have for us," and "none, you covered everything" is scored as low interest. Bring six written down, ask four or five, and take notes on the answers.

Questions that make you look like a colleague:

- What does the tech actually do here? Do techs draw blood, start IVs, run EKGs, apply splints?
- What does orientation look like, and how long is the precepted period?
- What is the tech-to-patient ratio on a typical night?
- How does scheduling work: self-scheduling or block, and how far out is it posted?
- What separates a tech who does well here from one who struggles?
- Is there a path to cross-train into triage or fast track?
- Does the system offer tuition reimbursement, and what is the eligibility waiting period?
- What is the biggest change the department is going through right now?
- What are the next steps, and when do you expect to decide?

The last one is not optional. It gives you the timeline that controls your follow-up.

> **Trap:** Do not ask in a first interview about time off, how soon you can transfer out, whether you have to do something unpleasant, or what happened to the last person in the role. All four are reasonable questions and all four are read as a warning sign at this stage.

## What to wear

Business casual, not scrubs, unless you were specifically told to wear scrubs for a shadow shift. Collared shirt, clean slacks, closed shoes, a belt. A tie is optional in most EDs and never wrong. Nails short and clean. Hair off the face.

Skip cologne and scented products entirely. Hospitals ask staff to be scent-free because patients with asthma and nausea react to it, and an interviewer notices.

Cover what you can cover; visible tattoos and small piercings are widely accepted in EDs now, but the first interview is not where you test the local policy.

## What to bring

- Three printed copies of the resume in a plain folder
- Copies of your certification cards: EMT, BLS, anything else
- Photo ID and, if you have it, your certification number written down
- A reference list of three people, each asked in advance and each with a phone and email
- A pen and a small notebook. Writing down an answer reads as seriousness
- The names and titles of your interviewers, so the thank-you email goes to the right people

## The logistics that sink people

Hospital parking is genuinely hard. Add 20 minutes for the garage and the walk, then arrive at the building 15 minutes early and at the desk 5 to 10 minutes early. Earlier than 15 is its own small imposition.

Phone off, not silent. A buzzing pocket is audible.

> **On shift:** The interview starts in the parking lot. The person you were short with at the front desk, in the elevator, or at security may be the person the manager asks about you afterward. This happens constantly and candidates never see it coming.

For a video interview: camera at eye level, a light source in front of you rather than a window behind you, plain background, wired internet if possible, and join 10 minutes early to test audio. Look at the camera lens when you speak, not at the faces on the screen. Keep a one-page cheat sheet of your six stories just off camera.
keyPoints: Bring six questions, ask four or five, and always ask about next steps and the decision timeline.
Do not ask about time off, transferring out, or the last person in the role during a first interview.
Business casual, not scrubs, and no scented products.
Bring three resumes, certification copies, a three-person reference list, and a notebook.
Add 20 minutes for hospital parking; be at the desk 5 to 10 minutes early with the phone off.

checks.q: The panel asks whether you have any questions. Which is the best one to ask?
choices: How much time off do I get in the first year?
What separates a tech who does well here from one who struggles?
Is there a lot of mandatory overtime?
What happened to the person who had this job before?
checks.why: It asks about performance in their department, gives you usable information, and signals you intend to be good at the job. Time off, overtime, and predecessor questions are legitimate but are read at this stage as looking for reasons to decline.

checks.q: You are told the interview is on the medical campus at 2 p.m. When should you plan to arrive at the garage?
choices: 1:55 p.m., since the desk is right inside
About 1:35 p.m., because hospital parking and the walk routinely take 20 minutes
1:00 p.m., to be safe
2:00 p.m. exactly
checks.why: Hospital garages fill, are far from the right entrance, and often require a security check-in. Arriving at the garage 25 minutes out puts you at the desk 5 to 10 minutes early. An hour early is an imposition on staff who have to find somewhere to put you.

checks.q: Why does the advice say phone off rather than silent?
choices: Hospitals block cell signals in clinical areas
Vibrate is still audible in a quiet room and is read as inattention
Silent mode still rings for alarms only
It is required by HIPAA
checks.why: A buzzing pocket is heard by everyone in a small room and interrupts an answer. It has nothing to do with HIPAA or signal blocking; it is purely about attention.

lessons.title: The first ninety days
lessons.body:
## What orientation actually is

Three stacked things, over roughly four to eight weeks.

**Hospital orientation**, 1 to 3 days in a classroom with every new hire in the system: HIPAA, safety, fire, infection control, payroll, badge, and a session on the electronic record.

**Department orientation**, where you learn the physical department, the supply rooms, the zones, and the people.

**Precepted shifts**, commonly 4 to 8 weeks or 6 to 12 shifts, working alongside an experienced tech who signs off your **competency checklist**: vital signs, 12-lead EKG, point-of-care glucose, specimen collection and labeling, urinary catheter if in scope, splinting, restraint monitoring, transport, CPR, safe patient handling. You cannot do a skill solo until that line is signed.

Most hospitals also run a **90-day probationary period**, during which the usual progressive discipline process does not apply and employment can end without it. Union contracts define this explicitly. Nothing about it is sinister; it just means the first three months are the ones that count double.

## How to earn trust faster than everyone else

None of this is clinical. All of it is noticed within two weeks.

- Be early. Ten minutes, every shift, so the person you relieve leaves on time.
- Answer a call light that is not your patient's. Never say "not my patient."
- Learn where everything is in week one. Draw an actual map of the supply room and the code cart contents.
- Restock and clean without being asked. It is the fastest reputation available in a hospital.
- Write down the names of the nurses in your zone at the start of every shift and use them.
- Close the loop out loud: "EKG on 12 is done, `2106`, it's on the rack, rate looked around 120." A task nobody knows you finished is a task you did not do.
- Ask for feedback at 30 days, in one sentence: "What is one thing I should be doing differently?" Then do it, visibly.

> **Key:** The tech everyone wants is not the one with the best hands in month one. It is the one whose work does not have to be checked and who says what they did and when.

## The mistakes new techs make

- Guessing instead of asking, to avoid looking new
- Over-promising to patients. Never say "the doctor will be right in." Say "I'll let your nurse know you're waiting"
- Hiding an error
- Being on a personal phone where patients and families can see it
- Talking about patients in the hallway, the elevator, or the cafeteria
- Charting at the end of the shift from memory, or copying the last set of vitals forward
- Taking a nurse's sharpness personally in the middle of a bad hour
- Standing between a agitated patient and the door
- Attempting a skill you are not signed off on, to be useful

> **On shift:** "I don't know, let me find out" has never ended a career. Pretending to know has ended many. Say it, then actually go find out and come back with the answer.

## When you make an error

You will. The response is fixed and it is not complicated.

1. Tell the nurse immediately. Not at the end of the shift, not after you think about it.
2. Address the patient's safety first, whatever that requires.
3. Chart what happened factually, in objective language, with real times. No speculation, no blame.
4. Complete the incident or safety report if the department uses one. It is a quality document, kept separate from the medical record.

Mislabeled specimens, a missed 15-minute restraint check, vitals charted on the wrong patient: what ends people is the delay and the concealment, not the mistake. Departments expect errors from new staff and have systems built to catch them. Those systems only work if you speak.
keyPoints: Orientation is hospital classroom days, department orientation, then 4 to 8 weeks of precepted shifts with a signed competency checklist.
A 90-day probationary period means the first three months count double.
Close the loop out loud on every task with what you did and the time you did it.
Never promise a patient that the provider is coming right in; say you will tell the nurse.
Report every error to the nurse immediately; concealment, not the error, is what ends jobs.

checks.q: You finish a 12-lead EKG on a chest pain patient. What must happen next?
choices: File it in the chart rack and continue your tasks
Hand it immediately to the provider or nurse and say the time it was taken
Wait for the provider to ask for it
Interpret it and report your reading to the nurse
checks.why: An EKG that nobody has looked at is worthless; a STEMI is identified by a provider reading it within minutes. Techs do not interpret, but they do hand it over with the time and say so out loud.

checks.q: Two hours into your shift you realize you charted a set of vitals under the wrong patient. What do you do?
choices: Leave it; the numbers were normal anyway
Tell the nurse right away, correct the record per policy, and file the safety report if required
Delete the entry quietly so no one sees it
Wait until the end of shift and tell the charge nurse then
checks.why: Wrong-patient documentation can drive real clinical decisions, and records are audited and versioned so quiet deletion is both impossible and a far worse offense. Immediate disclosure plus a policy-based correction is the expected response.

checks.q: During your precepted period, a nurse asks you to place a urinary catheter, a skill your competency checklist has not yet been signed off for. What is correct?
choices: Do it, since a nurse asked and it is within the tech role at this hospital
Say you are not signed off yet, offer to set up and assist, and ask her to sign you off or find someone who is
Refuse and walk away
Attempt it and ask her to watch
checks.why: The checklist is the hospital's legal record of what you are competent to do; performing an unsigned skill is unsafe and unprotected even with permission. Offering to assist and asking to be signed off solves her problem and advances your orientation.

lessons.title: Pay, differentials, and surviving shift work
lessons.body:
## What the job pays

Ranges move, so treat these as approximate and verify against the posting. In the South Jersey and Philadelphia market an ED tech generally runs about `$18` to `$26` an hour, with EMT certification plus a phlebotomy certificate landing you toward the upper half of a given posting's range. Per diem typically runs `$25` to `$34` with no benefits.

Then the differentials stack on top. Work the arithmetic once, because it changes which job is actually the better offer:

`$21.00` base, plus `$4.00` night, plus `$2.50` weekend, equals `$27.50` an hour. A Saturday night twelve is about `$330` before tax. Three twelves a week on nights is a different income from three twelves on days at the same posted base.

## What is actually negotiable

At most hospitals, and at every union hospital, the hourly rate comes off a published step grid. You cannot talk your way up a grid. You can sometimes move where you start on it.

Negotiable, in rough order of likelihood: starting step (credit for EMT certification, phlebotomy certificate, or prior patient-facing experience), shift assignment, start date, sign-on bonus, and when tuition reimbursement eligibility begins.

Ask once, politely, with a reason attached: "Given the EMT certification and the phlebotomy certificate, is there room to start at the next step?" Then accept the answer gracefully. One ask is professional. Two is a problem.

**Tuition reimbursement** is the lever that matters most for a long plan. Typical programs pay `$2,500` to `$5,250` per year; `$5,250` recurs because it is the IRS limit on employer education assistance that is not taxed as income. Expect an eligibility waiting period of 6 to 12 months, a minimum grade requirement, and sometimes a payback clause if you leave within a year of the last payment.

> **Key:** For someone taking prerequisite science courses, tuition reimbursement is often worth more than a dollar an hour. Ask about it in the interview, and confirm the waiting period in the offer letter.

## Nights: sleep is part of the job

Working nights is a physiological insult, and the people who last are the ones who treat daytime sleep as a scheduled obligation rather than something that happens if there is time.

- Blackout curtains, earplugs or a fan, phone on do-not-disturb with an exception for true emergencies
- A fixed sleep window, for example `0830` to `1530` after a `1900` to `0700` shift, kept the same every workday
- Caffeine has a half-life of about 5 hours, so half of a `0100` coffee is still circulating at `0600`. Last dose at least 6 hours before you intend to sleep
- A 20 to 30 minute nap before the shift is the highest-yield thing you can do. If you have more room, take a full 90-minute cycle instead. Avoid 45 to 60 minutes, which wakes you out of deep sleep feeling worse
- Sunglasses on the drive home; bright light during the first half of the shift
- On days off, keep an anchor of about 4 hours of sleep at the same clock time so your rhythm does not fully reset
- Melatonin `0.5` to `3 mg` has modest evidence for shift adaptation, and the low dose works about as well as the high one

Eat the main meal before the shift and keep the overnight food light and protein-based. A heavy meal at `0400` makes the last three hours worse. Exercise before shifts, not after; a hard workout at `0730` fights the sleep you need at `0830`.

## The part nobody warns you about

The emotional load is cumulative, not dramatic. Most techs are fine after the first bad trauma and quietly worn down eleven months later. Watch for the honest signals: dreading the drive in, flatness at home, needing alcohol to fall asleep, irritability with people who did nothing.

Use the post-incident debrief if the department runs one, and use the employee assistance program (EAP), which is free, confidential, and does not go in your personnel file. Talking to someone after a pediatric death is not weakness; it is maintenance.

> **On shift:** If you have worked nights properly for a year and still cannot sleep, that is information, not failure. Day shifts, evening shifts, and other departments exist, and internal transfers after a year are routine.
keyPoints: South Jersey and Philadelphia ED techs run roughly $18 to $26 an hour, per diem $25 to $34 without benefits; verify against the posting.
Differentials stack, so compute the effective rate for the shift you will really work.
The rate usually comes off a step grid; the starting step, shift, start date, and sign-on are the negotiable parts.
Tuition reimbursement commonly runs $2,500 to $5,250 a year and often beats a dollar an hour for someone taking prerequisites.
Caffeine's half-life is about 5 hours, so the last dose goes at least 6 hours before your planned sleep.

checks.q: Your base is $21.00 an hour with a $4.00 night differential and a $2.50 weekend differential. What do you earn for a 12-hour Saturday night shift, before tax?
choices: About $252
About $300
About $330
About $378
checks.why: Differentials stack onto the base: 21.00 plus 4.00 plus 2.50 is 27.50 an hour, times 12 hours is 330. Using the base alone gives 252, and counting only one differential gives 300.

checks.q: You work 1900 to 0700 and plan to sleep at 0830. When should your last caffeine be?
choices: No later than about 0230
0600 is fine since you will be tired anyway
Any time during the shift
Caffeine timing does not affect sleep in shift workers
checks.why: With a half-life near 5 hours, caffeine taken 6 or more hours before sleep has dropped substantially. A 0600 dose leaves most of it circulating at 0830. Fatigue does not neutralize the drug; it just masks the effect until you lie down.

checks.q: Which is the strongest reason to ask about tuition reimbursement during the interview?
choices: It signals you are planning to leave
It is often worth more than a dollar an hour to someone taking prerequisite courses, and the waiting period should be confirmed in the offer
It is legally required to be disclosed
It replaces the need to negotiate pay
checks.why: At $2,500 to $5,250 a year it can exceed the value of a small rate increase, and the 6 to 12 month eligibility period changes when you can start courses. Employers expect the question and it does not read as disloyalty.

lessons.title: Using the job to get into PA school
lessons.body:
## The hours are the point

PA programs weigh **patient care experience** (PCE) heavily, and they distinguish it from **healthcare experience** (HCE). PCE means you were hands-on and responsible for some part of a patient's care. HCE means you worked in healthcare without that direct role, like a scribe or a unit clerk. An ED tech job is close to the cleanest PCE there is.

Program minimums vary widely. Many set a floor of `500` to `2,000` hours; competitive applicants often show `1,000` to `3,000` or more. Every program publishes its own number, and the number is a floor rather than a target.

**Log from day one.** The application asks for start and end dates, job title, average hours per week, and a supervisor's name, title, email, and phone, and it verifies them. Keep a running spreadsheet and update it monthly.

> **Key:** Get your supervisor's personal email before either of you leaves. Reconstructing three years of hours from memory with a manager who has moved to another system is the most avoidable misery in this entire process.

## What to do inside the job

- **Get on the code team.** Volunteer for compressions, learn the cart drawer by drawer, and ask the educator whether the department will pay for ACLS. Techs who are useful in a code get invited into everything else.
- **Cross-train into triage.** Vitals, chief complaint, and watching acuity decisions being made is the single best free education in the building.
- **Cross-train into fast track.** Splints, wound care, suture setup, discharge teaching. More procedures per shift than anywhere else in the department.
- **Get fast and clean on the 12-lead.** Under 4 minutes from walking in to handing it over, every time, with correct lead placement. It is the skill your name gets attached to.
- **Become the tech who trains new techs.** Precepting is a responsibility, and asking for it is how a letter of recommendation gets written about leadership instead of attendance.

## Shadowing and letters

Shadowing hours are counted separately from work hours, and most programs want them, with `20` to `40` hours of PA shadowing a common expectation. You are about to work next to PAs every shift, which is an access problem other applicants pay for.

Ask directly, on a slow night, in one sentence: "Would you be open to me shadowing you on one of my days off?" Most say yes. Track the date, hours, the PA's name, and the specialty.

Letters of recommendation usually run three: a PA you worked with closely, a physician or your direct supervisor, and a science faculty member. Ask at 12 months or more of working together, ask in person, give them an easy out, and hand them your resume, your hour log, and the deadline.

## The academic half

The common prerequisites are anatomy and physiology I and II with labs, microbiology with lab, general chemistry, organic chemistry or biochemistry, statistics, and psychology. Requirements differ by program, so build a spreadsheet of five to ten target programs and their exact lists before you register for anything.

Schedule realistically. A night shift plus an `0800` lab is a bad combination that ends in a withdrawn course. One or two courses per semester alongside three twelves is normal and sustainable.

> **Trap:** A withdrawal or a C in anatomy hurts more than a slow schedule does. Take fewer courses and earn the grade.

The centralized application, CASPA, opens in late April, and most programs use rolling admissions, so submitting in the first six weeks is a genuine advantage over an identical application sent in September. Whether the GRE or PA-CAT is required varies by program and changes, so verify each one the year you apply.

Two to three years as an ED tech while finishing prerequisites is not a detour. It is one of the most common and most respected paths into a PA program, because it produces an applicant who has actually touched patients.
keyPoints: PA programs count patient care experience separately from healthcare experience; ED tech work is direct PCE.
Program floors commonly run 500 to 2,000 hours, with competitive applicants often at 1,000 to 3,000 or more.
Log dates, hours, and supervisor contact information monthly, because the application verifies them.
Shadowing hours are separate from work hours; 20 to 40 hours of PA shadowing is a common expectation.
CASPA opens in late April and most programs use rolling admissions, so apply in the first six weeks.

checks.q: How does a PA application classify ED tech work?
choices: Healthcare experience, because you are not licensed
Patient care experience, because you are hands-on and responsible for part of the patient's care
Volunteer experience
It does not count unless you are a paramedic
checks.why: Patient care experience means direct, hands-on responsibility for patient care. Techs take vitals, draw blood, run EKGs, and perform procedures, which is squarely PCE. Scribes and unit clerks are the classic healthcare-experience roles.

checks.q: Why does applying to a rolling-admissions PA program in the first six weeks after CASPA opens matter?
choices: Early applications receive extra points
Seats and interview slots fill as the cycle runs, so an identical application is weaker in September
The application fee is lower early
Prerequisites are not checked early in the cycle
checks.why: Rolling admissions means files are reviewed and offers made continuously. There is no bonus for being early and no discount; the advantage is simply that more interview slots and seats still exist.

checks.q: You are working three twelve-hour night shifts a week and want to finish prerequisites. What is the sensible plan?
choices: Take four courses per semester to finish in a year
Take one or two courses per semester and protect the grades
Take only online courses with no labs
Stop working until prerequisites are complete
checks.why: Grade quality in anatomy, physiology, and chemistry matters more to admissions than speed, and a withdrawal or a C costs more than an extra semester. Many programs also require in-person labs, and stopping work sacrifices the patient care hours that make the application competitive.

cards.front: Name four job titles that describe the same ED technician role.
cards.back: ED technician, ER technician, patient care technician - emergency (PCT-ED), clinical technician or clinical associate, emergency care technician, and nursing assistant - emergency.

cards.front: How is the tech role different at an academic Level I trauma center versus a community ED?
cards.back: Level I: higher acuity, residents who claim procedures, heavy protocol, strong teaching culture. Community ED: smaller staff, techs own more tasks such as draws, EKGs, splints and sometimes IVs, and you get hands on sooner.

cards.front: What is a freestanding ED and what happens to sick patients there?
cards.back: A full emergency department with no hospital attached. It screens, treats and stabilizes, then discharges or transfers anyone needing admission. Still bound by EMTALA, still sees true emergencies.

cards.front: Which hospital is the only Level I trauma center in South Jersey?
cards.back: Cooper University Hospital in Camden. It is the academic Level I referral center for the region.

cards.front: Why does tech scope vary between two hospitals with identical job postings?
cards.back: Scope is set department by department by nursing leadership and policy, not by the title. One ED lets techs draw blood and start IVs; the next lets techs touch no needles at all.

cards.front: What is the single most useful question to ask about the role in an interview?
cards.back: What does the tech actually do here: do techs draw blood, start IVs, run EKGs, apply splints? It tells you what skills the job builds and marks you as someone who thinks about the work.

cards.front: How does someone become a certified EMT in New Jersey?
cards.back: Complete an approved EMT course, then pass the National Registry cognitive exam and the state-approved psychomotor exam (the National Registry does not administer the EMT-level psychomotor exam), then hold certification through NJ OEMS. Course runs about 3 to 6 months.

cards.front: Which CPR card do hospitals actually accept, and how long is it valid?
cards.back: AHA BLS Provider (or American Red Cross BLS) with an in-person skills check, valid 2 years. Online-only or lay CPR certificates are rejected at employee health.

cards.front: Is phlebotomy certification legally required to draw blood in New Jersey?
cards.back: No. New Jersey does not license phlebotomists. A certificate such as the NHA CPT is still worth having because it shortens your training and can raise your starting pay step.

cards.front: What is the hepatitis B vaccine schedule and why does it affect your start date?
cards.back: Doses at 0, 1 and 6 months, then a surface antibody titer 1 to 2 months after the last dose. That is 7 to 8 months total, so an incomplete series is a common reason a start date slips.

cards.front: What is the difference between a two-step TB skin test and an IGRA?
cards.back: The two-step tuberculin skin test needs four visits over 1 to 3 weeks (place, read, repeat). An IGRA such as QuantiFERON is a single blood draw at one visit.

cards.front: What is an N95 fit test and how often is it required?
cards.back: A roughly 20-minute test at employee health confirming a specific respirator model seals on your face. OSHA requires it at hire and annually, and after facial changes such as significant weight change.

cards.front: Does New Jersey cannabis legalization protect you from a pre-employment drug screen at a hospital?
cards.back: No. NJ law limits adverse action based on a cannabis test alone, but hospitals holding federal contracts and safety-sensitive employers still test and still rescind offers. Do not assume protection.

cards.front: List the four contingencies that can cancel a hospital job offer.
cards.back: Criminal background check and employment verification, drug screen, employee health clearance including immunizations and TB, and certification or license verification.

cards.front: What does 0.6 FTE mean in hours per week?
cards.back: About 24 hours a week, typically two twelve-hour shifts. 1.0 FTE is 40 hours (or 36 at twelve-hour hospitals), 0.9 is 36, and 0.5 is 20.

cards.front: What does per diem (PRN) status mean for pay, benefits and commitment?
cards.back: Higher base rate, no benefits, and a written minimum such as two shifts a month plus a holiday. It gives the least orientation and precepted time, which is why it is a poor first hospital job.

cards.front: At roughly what FTE do hospital benefits usually begin?
cards.back: Commonly around 0.5 to 0.6 FTE, or about 20 hours a week, but the threshold is set by the system, so read the posting and confirm in the offer letter.

cards.front: Give typical ranges for night, evening and weekend shift differentials.
cards.back: Evening about $1.50 to $3.00 per hour, night about $2.00 to $5.00, weekend about $1.50 to $4.00. They stack with each other on top of the base rate.

cards.front: What is the difference between self-scheduling and block scheduling?
cards.back: Self-scheduling lets you request your own shifts within rules before the schedule is built. Block scheduling assigns a fixed repeating pattern. Self-scheduling is worth real quality of life.

cards.front: What changes when an ED tech position is a union position in New Jersey?
cards.back: Pay comes off a published step scale by years of service, the probationary period is contractually defined, seniority governs shift bids and time off, and dues come out of your check. HPAE and JNESO are the common unions.

cards.front: A posting says 'EMT preferred, 1 year patient care experience required.' You have EMT and no hospital experience. What do you do?
cards.back: Apply. 'Preferred' is not required, and experience minimums are routinely waived for certified EMTs. Screening yourself out is the most common self-inflicted mistake in a job search.

cards.front: What formatting choices break applicant tracking software?
cards.back: Two columns, tables, text boxes, graphics and skill bars, photos, and content placed in headers or footers. Use one column, standard section headers, and a common font.

cards.front: Where should certifications appear on a first hospital resume, and with what detail?
cards.back: At the top, above experience, with certification numbers and expiration dates, for example NJ EMT-B exp 03/2029 and AHA BLS Provider exp 06/2028. It answers the screener's gating question immediately.

cards.front: Why is an objective statement a mistake on a hospital resume?
cards.back: It occupies the most valuable space on the page and tells the manager nothing specific. Use those lines for certifications or a two-line concrete summary instead.

cards.front: What is the bullet formula for a resume line, and what makes a bullet invisible?
cards.back: Action verb, what you did, the scale, the result. A bullet without a number is invisible: 'handled complaints' says nothing, 'resolved 20 to 30 escalated complaints weekly' describes a person.

cards.front: How do you translate 'calmed down angry customers' into hospital language?
cards.back: De-escalated 20 or more confrontations per week without security involvement. De-escalation is a named ED competency, so use the word and attach a frequency.

cards.front: Why mirror the job posting's exact wording in your resume?
cards.back: Applicant tracking software matches your text against the requisition. Writing 'bedside lab tests' when the posting says 'point-of-care testing' can cost you the keyword match entirely.

cards.front: List the steps from application to first day at a hospital.
cards.back: Portal application, recruiter phone screen, panel interview, sometimes a shadow shift, verbal then written contingent offer, employee health clearance, start date. Typically 4 to 8 weeks total.

cards.front: Who is usually on an ED tech interview panel?
cards.back: The ED manager or clinical director plus a charge nurse, sometimes a clinical educator or a senior tech. Expect mostly behavioral questions over 30 to 60 minutes.

cards.front: What are the rules for a shadow shift?
cards.back: Observation only, usually 2 to 4 unpaid hours. No patient contact, no touching equipment, stay out of doorways, ask questions during lulls, learn names. Staff feedback goes back to the manager.

cards.front: When is it safe to resign your current job?
cards.back: After the written offer is in hand and the contingencies (background check, drug screen, employee health, certification verification) have cleared. Never on a verbal offer.

cards.front: What is the correct follow-up rhythm after an interview?
cards.back: A thank-you email within 24 hours to each interviewer, three to five sentences naming something specific. Then one follow-up three days after the timeline they gave you. Then stop.

cards.front: Name four things to do when leaving a retail or service job so the reference survives.
cards.back: Two weeks in writing, tell the manager before any coworker, work the shifts you committed to, and get the manager's personal email and cell plus an explicit yes to being a reference.

cards.front: What does STAR stand for and how long should the answer run?
cards.back: Situation, Task, Action, Result. One sentence, one sentence, three or four sentences, one sentence with a number or outcome. About 60 to 90 seconds total.

cards.front: Why prepare six stories instead of memorizing twenty-five answers?
cards.back: Behavioral panels re-slice the same material. Six stories (angry person, a mistake, teaching someone, prioritizing under load, a disagreement, going beyond for one person) cover nearly every question asked.

cards.front: What are the three beats of a good 'tell me about yourself' answer?
cards.back: Where you are now and what you hold, why emergency medicine specifically, and what you want to be doing in a few years. Ninety seconds, no childhood, no biography.

cards.front: How do you answer 'tell me about a mistake you made'?
cards.back: Pick a real, small-stakes error. Own it in one flat sentence, then spend the answer on what you did immediately, who you told, and the change that prevents a recurrence. Refusing to name one fails the question.

cards.front: What are the three parts of a strong answer to the out-of-scope question?
cards.back: Decline the task, keep the relationship, solve her problem: 'I'm not signed off on that, what do you need to happen, here's what I can do, and I'll find someone who can do the rest.'

cards.front: What does a strong 'how do you prioritize' answer contain?
cards.back: A stated rule (life threats, then time-critical orders such as a 10-minute EKG or sepsis labs, then longest waiting) plus the winning sentence: 'and I tell the nurse what I am not going to get to.'

cards.front: How do you answer the weakness question without sounding evasive?
cards.back: Name a real limitation plus the system that contains it, such as moving fast and skipping notes, now fixed with a brain sheet and charting times as you go. Avoid disguised strengths and 'I don't have one'.

cards.front: The recruiter asks what pay you are looking for. What is the move?
cards.back: Give a researched range and redirect: roughly $20 to $25 an hour for this role and area depending on certification, then say you care more about schedule and training. Avoid naming one number first.

cards.front: Name four strong questions to ask an ED interview panel.
cards.back: What does the tech actually do here; how long is the precepted orientation; what separates a tech who does well from one who struggles; is there a path to cross-train into triage or fast track.

cards.front: Which questions should you not ask in a first ED interview?
cards.back: Time off, how soon you can transfer out, whether you have to do something unpleasant, and what happened to your predecessor. All reasonable later, all read as a warning sign now.

cards.front: What do you wear to an ED tech interview, and what do you leave off?
cards.back: Business casual: collared shirt, clean slacks, closed shoes. Not scrubs unless told. No cologne or scented products, nails short, hair off the face.

cards.front: What should you physically bring to the interview?
cards.back: Three printed resumes in a folder, copies of certification cards, photo ID, a three-person reference list with phone and email, a pen and notebook, and the interviewers' names.

cards.front: How early should you arrive for a hospital interview, and why?
cards.back: At the garage about 25 minutes early because parking and the walk take 20, then at the desk 5 to 10 minutes early. More than 15 minutes early at the desk is an imposition on staff.

cards.front: What are the three stacked parts of ED tech orientation and how long do they run?
cards.back: Hospital classroom orientation 1 to 3 days, department orientation, then 4 to 8 weeks or 6 to 12 precepted shifts with a competency checklist signed by a preceptor or educator.

cards.front: What is a competency checklist and what does it control?
cards.back: The hospital's signed record of which skills you may perform alone: vitals, 12-lead, point-of-care glucose, specimen collection, splinting, restraint monitoring, transport, CPR. Unsigned means you do not do it solo.

cards.front: What is a 90-day probationary period?
cards.back: The first three months, during which the normal progressive discipline process does not apply and employment can end without it. Union contracts define it explicitly. It means the first 90 days count double.

cards.front: What does 'closing the loop' mean for a tech, and give an example.
cards.back: Telling the nurse what you did and when, out loud. 'EKG on room 12 done at 2106, it's on the rack, rate looked around 120.' A task nobody knows you finished is a task you did not do.

cards.front: Name five habits that build a new tech's reputation in the first two weeks.
cards.back: Arrive ten minutes early, answer call lights that are not yours, learn where everything is, restock and clean unasked, and use the nurses' names in your zone.

cards.front: Why should you never tell a patient 'the doctor will be right in'?
cards.back: You cannot control it, and a broken promise is the most common trigger for family anger later. Say instead that you will let the nurse know they are waiting, then actually do it.

cards.front: You made an error. What are the four steps?
cards.back: Tell the nurse immediately, address patient safety first, chart what happened factually with real times, and complete the incident or safety report. Delay and concealment end jobs; errors usually do not.

cards.front: What is the approximate pay range for an ED tech in the South Jersey and Philadelphia area?
cards.back: Roughly $18 to $26 an hour depending on system, certification and experience; per diem about $25 to $34 with no benefits. Ranges move, so verify against the posting.

cards.front: Base is $21.00, night differential $4.00, weekend $2.50. What does a 12-hour Saturday night pay before tax?
cards.back: $27.50 an hour times 12 hours, about $330. Differentials stack on the base, which is why you compare jobs on the shift you will actually work.

cards.front: In a hospital offer, what is usually negotiable and what is not?
cards.back: The hourly rate usually is not, because it comes off a step grid. Negotiable: starting step, shift assignment, start date, sign-on bonus, and tuition reimbursement eligibility timing. Ask once, with a reason.

cards.front: How much tuition reimbursement do hospitals typically offer, and why is $5,250 a common number?
cards.back: Commonly $2,500 to $5,250 a year. $5,250 is the IRS limit on employer education assistance that is not taxed as income. Expect a 6 to 12 month waiting period and a grade minimum.

cards.front: Caffeine's half-life is about 5 hours. What does that mean for a 1900 to 0700 shift?
cards.back: Half of a 0100 coffee is still circulating at 0600. Take the last dose at least 6 hours before your planned sleep, so by about 0230 if you intend to sleep at 0830.

cards.front: What nap length should a night worker take, and which length should be avoided?
cards.back: 20 to 30 minutes before the shift, or a full 90-minute cycle if there is room. Avoid 45 to 60 minutes, which wakes you out of deep sleep feeling worse than before.

cards.front: What is anchor sleep and why does it matter on days off?
cards.back: Keeping about 4 hours of sleep at the same clock time on days off so the circadian rhythm does not fully reset to days. It makes the return to nights far less brutal.

cards.front: What are the honest warning signs that the emotional load of ED work is accumulating?
cards.back: Dreading the drive in, flatness at home, needing alcohol to fall asleep, and irritability with people who did nothing. Use post-incident debriefs and the EAP, which is free and confidential.

cards.front: What is the difference between patient care experience and healthcare experience on a PA application?
cards.back: PCE means hands-on responsibility for part of a patient's care, such as an ED tech. HCE means working in healthcare without that direct role, such as a scribe or unit clerk.

cards.front: How many patient care hours do PA programs expect?
cards.back: Minimums commonly fall between 500 and 2,000 hours, and competitive applicants often show 1,000 to 3,000 or more. Every program publishes its own floor, and a floor is not a target.

cards.front: What information must you log monthly for PA application hour verification?
cards.back: Start and end dates, job title, average hours per week, and the supervisor's name, title, email and phone. Applications verify it, so get personal contact details before anyone moves jobs.

cards.front: Name four ways to build a PA application from inside an ED tech job.
cards.back: Get on the code team and learn the cart, cross-train into triage and fast track, get a clean 12-lead under 4 minutes every time, and become the tech who precepts new techs.

cards.front: How do shadowing hours differ from work hours, and how many are expected?
cards.back: Shadowing is observation, logged separately from paid patient care hours. 20 to 40 hours of PA shadowing is a common expectation. Record date, hours, the PA's name and specialty.

quiz.q: You are searching a large health system's career site for technician work in the emergency department and find no results for 'ED tech'. What is the best next step?
choices: Search the variants: patient care technician, clinical associate, emergency care technician, and the words emergency and technician separately
Call the ED directly and ask to speak to the manager
Wait until the system posts under that exact title
Apply to a nursing assistant role on an inpatient floor instead
quiz.why: The same job is posted under at least six titles and many postings never use the word 'tech'. Cold-calling a manager bypasses a portal that legally records applications, and waiting for an exact title means missing the market entirely.

quiz.q: An applicant wants the most hands-on procedural experience per shift as a new tech. Which setting most likely delivers it?
choices: A community ED where techs draw blood, run EKGs and apply splints
An academic Level I trauma center with a large residency program
A freestanding ED with one tech per shift and low acuity
An inpatient medical-surgical floor
quiz.why: Community EDs have no residents competing for procedures and give techs a wide task list with real volume. Level I centers route procedures to residents. A freestanding ED gives variety but far fewer patients, and an inpatient floor is a different job.

quiz.q: A posting requires 'current BLS'. The applicant holds a CPR card earned entirely online with no skills session. What happens?
choices: It is accepted because the content is identical
It is accepted if it is less than 2 years old
It is accepted provisionally for 90 days
It is rejected at employee health, because hospitals require a healthcare-provider BLS card with an in-person skills evaluation
quiz.why: Hospitals require AHA BLS Provider or Red Cross BLS with a hands-on skills check; blended HeartCode counts only when the skills session was completed. Online-only cards have no psychomotor verification and are rejected regardless of recency.

quiz.q: An applicant plans to apply to ED tech jobs in about three months. Which task should be started today because it takes the longest?
choices: The N95 fit test
The hepatitis B vaccine series
The BLS Provider course
The background check
quiz.why: Hepatitis B runs 0, 1 and 6 months plus a titer 1 to 2 months later, roughly 7 to 8 months. The fit test takes 20 minutes, BLS takes a day, and the background check is run by the employer after the offer.
