quiz.q: An applicant in New Jersey says a positive cannabis screen cannot cost him a hospital job because cannabis is legal in the state. What is the accurate response?
choices: He is correct; state law prohibits any adverse action
He is correct as long as he has a medical card
State law limits adverse action based on a test alone, but hospitals with federal contracts and safety-sensitive employers still test and still rescind offers
Hospitals no longer test for cannabis in New Jersey
quiz.why: Legalization changed state employment protections but did not remove employer testing, and federal contractors and safety-sensitive roles operate under separate obligations. A medical card does not compel a hospital to hire, and hospitals continue to screen.

quiz.q: A posting reads '0.9 FTE, nights, every other weekend, 12-hour shifts.' How many hours per week and how many shifts is that?
choices: 36 hours, three shifts
24 hours, two shifts
40 hours, four shifts
20 hours, two shifts
quiz.why: 0.9 FTE is 36 hours, which at 12 hours per shift is three shifts per week. 24 hours would be 0.6, 40 hours would be 1.0 on an eight-hour schedule, and 20 hours would be 0.5.

quiz.q: A new graduate EMT is offered a per diem ED tech position and a 0.6 FTE position at another hospital for slightly less per hour. Which is the better first job and why?
choices: Per diem, because the higher hourly rate compounds over a year
The 0.6 FTE, because scheduled staff receive full orientation and precepted shifts, which a new tech needs most
Per diem, because it offers more schedule flexibility for prerequisite courses
Either, since orientation is identical for all statuses
quiz.why: Per diem pays more precisely because it carries no benefits and minimal training investment; orientation and precepted shifts are what convert a certification into competence. Flexibility is real but worth little if you never got trained.

quiz.q: Two offers arrive. Hospital A: $22.50 base, day shift, no differentials. Hospital B: $21.00 base, night shift with $4.00 night differential, every other weekend with $2.50 weekend differential. Which comparison is correct?
choices: A pays more, because its base rate is higher
They are equivalent, since differentials are discretionary
B pays materially more on the shifts actually worked, $25.00 on weeknights and $27.50 on weekend nights
B pays less because night shifts are shorter
quiz.why: Differentials are paid automatically for hours worked and stack with each other, so B's effective rates are $25.00 and $27.50 against A's $22.50. Comparing posted base rates hides a difference worth thousands of dollars per year.

quiz.q: A candidate submits a visually striking two-column resume with a headshot, skill rating bars, and contact information in the page header. Weeks pass with no response. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The applicant tracking system parsed the layout into scrambled text and may have dropped the header contact information entirely
The manager considered the design unprofessional
Hospital portals reject files over one page
Headshots are prohibited by federal hiring law
quiz.why: Parsers read across columns, discard text boxes and often ignore header and footer regions, so the resume never becomes searchable text. Taste is a secondary issue, page limits are not usually enforced technically, and headshots are discouraged but not illegal.

quiz.q: Which resume bullet best translates shift-lead retail work for an ED tech application?
choices: Excellent interpersonal skills and a passion for helping others
Responsible for customer service, scheduling, and other duties as assigned
Worked in a fast-paced environment with a team-oriented mindset
Trained and onboarded 14 new employees and wrote the shift checklist still in use
quiz.why: It names a concrete action, a number, and a durable result, and training others is directly relevant to precepting and teamwork. The other three are adjectives and recycled job-description language that every applicant submits.

quiz.q: An applicant has completed a phlebotomy course but has not yet taken the certification exam. How should the resume handle it?
choices: List 'Certified Phlebotomy Technician' since the course is complete
List the course as completed with the date and note the certification exam is scheduled
Omit it entirely until the certificate arrives
List it under Certifications with an expected expiration date
quiz.why: Listing a credential you do not hold is falsification and fails verification, which ends the application permanently. Omitting it discards real training. Stating training completed plus an exam date is both accurate and useful.

quiz.q: A candidate receives an enthusiastic verbal offer over the phone and is asked to start in three weeks. What should happen before he resigns his current job?
choices: Nothing; a verbal offer from a manager is binding
He should resign immediately so he can start on time
He should wait for the written offer and for the background check, drug screen and employee health clearance to clear
He should resign but ask to stay on as needed
quiz.why: Hospital offers are contingent by default and do fail at screening or verification, which would leave him with no job at all. The written offer also fixes title, FTE, rate, shift and start date in a form you can hold them to.

quiz.q: During a 3-hour shadow shift the tech you are following is pulled into a code and asks you to grab a set of vitals on room 6. What do you do?
choices: Decline politely, explain you are observing only and are not yet an employee, and offer to find another staff member
Take the vitals, since you are EMT certified and it helps
Take the vitals but do not chart them
Leave the department to avoid being asked again
quiz.why: You are not credentialed, oriented or covered by the hospital, so any patient contact is a liability problem regardless of your certification. Declining while solving the problem is exactly the judgment they are watching for; leaving abandons the situation.

quiz.q: It has been 16 days since a strong panel interview and no one has responded to a polite follow-up sent on day 10. What is the best action?
choices: Send a second follow-up email and then call the manager directly
Assume rejection and withdraw the application
Contact HR to ask who else is being considered
Wait, keep applying elsewhere, and treat hospital timelines of several weeks as normal
quiz.why: Requisitions routinely take weeks and often must clear internal or union bidding before external candidates are reviewed. One follow-up was appropriate; repeated contact reads as anxiety and does not move a requisition, and asking about other candidates is inappropriate.

quiz.q: Asked 'tell me about a time you handled an angry customer,' a candidate describes a confrontation and ends with 'and I proved to her that the policy was clear, so she stopped arguing.' What is the main weakness?
choices: The story is too short
Retail examples are not accepted in hospital interviews
The candidate should have escalated to a manager
The result is being right rather than the person being calmed, which is the opposite of the de-escalation skill the ED is testing
quiz.why: De-escalation is measured by whether the other person came down, not by who was correct. An ED wants someone who absorbs anger without needing to win. Retail examples are entirely appropriate, and escalating is not automatically better.

quiz.q: In the interview you are asked, 'What would you do if a nurse asked you to give a patient their oral medication?' Which answer is best?
choices: I would give it, since the nurse is accountable for the order
I would tell her medications are not in my scope, ask what she needs to happen, offer to do anything else for that patient, and help get her another nurse
I would tell her that is a nursing task and go back to my assignment
I would document that she asked and report it to the manager
quiz.why: Medication administration is outside the tech scope regardless of who asks or who is accountable. Declining the task while asking what she needs, offering what you can do, and finding another nurse protects the scope line and the working relationship at once. Flat refusal damages the team, and reporting first skips the patient's actual need.

quiz.q: Which prioritization answer is strongest in an ED tech interview?
choices: I handle life threats first, then time-critical orders like a 10-minute EKG or sepsis labs, then the longest waiting, and I tell the nurse out loud what I am not going to get to
I do whatever the nurse asks first, in the order asked
I make a list and work through it steadily without stopping
I ask the charge nurse to prioritize for me each time
quiz.why: It states a rule, names real clocks, and adds the communication step that prevents a missed task from becoming a patient harm. Working strictly in the order asked ignores acuity, a steady list ignores urgency, and delegating every decision upward is not workable at volume.

quiz.q: A recruiter opens the phone screen with 'what pay are you looking for?' What is the best response?
choices: Whatever you think is fair
A researched range for the role and area, then a redirect to schedule and training
A single number at the top of the market
I would rather not discuss pay until the offer stage
quiz.why: A range shows preparation without anchoring you to one number, and redirecting to schedule and training keeps the conversation on fit. Deferring entirely frustrates a screen designed to check alignment, and a single high number can end the screen.

quiz.q: At the end of a panel interview you are asked whether you have questions. Which choice is the strongest?
choices: No, I think you covered everything
How much vacation time do techs get in the first year?
How long is the precepted orientation, and what separates a tech who does well here from one who struggles?
Is mandatory overtime common here?
quiz.why: It asks about training and performance in their department, produces information you can use, and signals intent to be good at the job. 'No questions' scores as low interest, and vacation or overtime questions at this stage read as looking for reasons to decline.

quiz.q: A candidate is invited to a 2 p.m. interview on a large medical campus and arrives at the main garage at 1:55 p.m. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: He arrives early and relaxed
He arrives late or flustered, because the garage, the walk and security check-in routinely take 20 minutes
Parking is validated so timing does not matter
Late arrival is acceptable if he apologizes
quiz.why: Hospital garages fill, are often far from the correct entrance, and frequently require a security desk stop. Planning to be at the garage roughly 25 minutes early puts you at the interviewer's desk 5 to 10 minutes early, which is the target.

quiz.q: A candidate is polite and impressive during the panel but was curt with the security guard and the unit secretary on the way in. What is the likely consequence?
choices: It may cost him the job, because managers routinely ask staff how a candidate treated them
None; only the panel's opinion counts
It only matters if he is hired
Security and clerical staff are not permitted to give feedback
quiz.why: ED managers hire for team behavior and deliberately ask the people the candidate did not think mattered. How someone treats staff with no power over them is the most reliable available signal, and it is used.

quiz.q: It is day 12 of orientation. A nurse asks the new tech to insert a urinary catheter, a skill not yet signed off on his competency checklist. What is correct?
choices: Perform it, since a licensed nurse authorized it
Perform it under her direct observation to get the experience
State that the skill is not yet signed off, offer to set up and assist, and ask to be signed off or for someone qualified to perform it
Refuse and report the request to the educator
quiz.why: The competency checklist is the hospital's legal record of what you may do unsupervised; a nurse's verbal permission does not replace it. Assisting is appropriate and advances your orientation, while a flat refusal plus a report solves nothing for the patient.

quiz.q: Near the end of a busy shift a new tech realizes he documented a set of vital signs on the wrong patient two hours earlier. The values were within normal limits. What should he do?
choices: Nothing, since the values were normal and no harm occurred
Delete the entry so the chart is clean
Note it verbally in handoff at shift change
Tell the nurse immediately, correct the record according to policy, and complete a safety report if required
quiz.why: Wrong-patient data can drive real decisions, including a false reassurance that a deteriorating patient was stable. Records are versioned and audited, so quiet deletion is both impossible and a far more serious offense, and waiting until handoff is a two-hour delay in a safety issue.

quiz.q: A family member asks the tech when the doctor will see their mother. Which reply is best?
choices: The doctor will be right in
I don't know, you'll have to ask the nurse
I can't tell you exactly when, but I'm going to tell her nurse right now that you're waiting, and I'll come back and let you know what I hear
It depends how many emergencies come in
quiz.why: It is honest about uncertainty, commits to a specific action you control, and promises a return. Promising the provider is imminent creates the broken expectation that drives most family anger, and deflecting without acting abandons the family.

quiz.q: Which behavior most reliably builds a new tech's reputation in the first two weeks?
choices: Attempting advanced skills to show capability
Restocking rooms and answering call lights for patients who are not assigned to you
Staying quiet and only doing assigned tasks
Correcting nurses when their documentation looks wrong
quiz.why: Visible, unglamorous work that makes other people's shifts easier is the fastest reputation available in a hospital. Attempting unsigned skills is unsafe, minimal compliance is forgettable, and correcting licensed staff in week one is a social error even when you are right.

quiz.q: A hospital offers $20.50 an hour off a published union step scale. The candidate holds EMT certification and a phlebotomy certificate. What is the realistic negotiation?
choices: Ask for $24.00 an hour, since the rate is always negotiable
Accept without asking, since union rates are fixed and asking is inappropriate
Decline and apply to non-union hospitals only
Ask once whether the certifications qualify for a higher starting step, and ask about shift assignment, start date and tuition reimbursement eligibility
quiz.why: A step grid fixes the rate per step but the entry step often credits certifications and prior experience. One polite ask with a reason attached is professional. Demanding a rate outside the grid is not possible, and never asking leaves a real step on the table.

quiz.q: A tech working 1900 to 0700 plans to sleep at 0830 after the drive home. He drinks a large coffee at 0530 to finish charting. What is the predictable effect?
choices: With a half-life near 5 hours, most of the dose is still circulating at 0830, fragmenting the daytime sleep he needs
None, because fatigue overrides caffeine
It improves sleep quality by preventing overtiredness
Caffeine does not affect sleep when taken during daylight
quiz.why: Caffeine's half-life of roughly 5 hours means a 0530 dose is barely reduced by 0830. Fatigue masks the stimulant effect until you lie down, and daytime sleep is already fragile because it fights the circadian drive toward wakefulness.

quiz.q: Eleven months into night shift a tech notices he dreads the drive in, feels flat at home, and has started drinking to fall asleep. What is the appropriate response?
choices: Push through, since these feelings are normal in emergency work
Resign from the department immediately
Treat it as cumulative occupational stress: use post-incident debriefs and the employee assistance program, and consider a shift change
Request a transfer to a higher-acuity department for more stimulation
quiz.why: These are recognized signs of accumulating occupational stress, and EAP access is free, confidential and outside the personnel file. Pushing through is how it becomes worse, abrupt resignation forfeits options, and higher acuity increases the load rather than relieving it.

quiz.q: A PA applicant has 1,800 hours as an ED tech and 1,200 hours as a medical scribe. How will most programs classify these?
choices: Both count fully as patient care experience
The tech hours count as patient care experience; the scribe hours count as healthcare experience
Both count as healthcare experience since neither role is licensed
Only the scribe hours count, because they involve documentation
quiz.why: Patient care experience requires hands-on responsibility for part of a patient's care, which the tech role has and the scribe role does not. Licensure is not the dividing line, and documentation work is the classic example of healthcare rather than patient care experience.

quiz.q: An ED tech plans to apply to PA school in two years. Which combination best builds the application from inside the job?
choices: Pick up maximum overtime to accumulate hours as fast as possible
Transfer to an inpatient floor for a broader clinical picture
Focus entirely on prerequisite coursework and work per diem
Cross-train into triage and fast track, join the code team, arrange PA shadowing on days off, and log hours and supervisor contacts monthly
quiz.why: It builds skill breadth, relationships that become letters, separately counted shadowing hours, and a verifiable hour log. Raw overtime adds hours past the point of diminishing returns, an inpatient transfer gives less procedural exposure, and per diem sacrifices both hours and training.

scenarios.title: The panel interview
scenarios.intro:
Tuesday, 1400. A community hospital in Camden County, conference room off the ED. Three people across the table: the ED clinical director, a night charge nurse, and the department educator. The posting was for an ED tech, 0.9 FTE, nights, every other weekend.

You brought three copies of your resume, your EMT and BLS cards, and six questions written on the inside of a folder. The director opens a folder of her own, uncaps a pen, and starts.

Each step is one of her questions. Pick the answer that would actually land.

choices.text: "I'm a certified EMT with BLS, I've spent the last few years in service work managing people and difficult situations, and I came to emergency medicine because I want to be in the room when it matters. Long term I'm working toward PA school, and this is the job that builds the hands."
choices.feedback: Ninety seconds, three beats: what you hold, why emergency medicine, where you are going. The PA goal is stated without making the job sound like a waiting room.

choices.text: "I was born in Camden, went to school here, worked a bunch of jobs, and I've always wanted to do something in medicine since I was a kid."
choices.feedback: This is a biography, and it never reaches the present. The question is an invitation to frame yourself professionally, and a childhood answer wastes the only uninterrupted 90 seconds you get.

choices.text: "Honestly, I'm just looking to get my foot in the door somewhere. I'll take whatever you've got."
choices.feedback: Availability and eagerness are not the same as fit. This tells a panel you would take any job in the building, which makes it hard to argue you want this one.

choices.text: "I'm applying to PA school in two years, so I need patient care hours, and this job is the most efficient way to get them."
choices.feedback: True, and exactly the sentence that sinks candidates. The panel hears a person who will leave, has no stake in the department, and views patients as a counter. Say the goal, but anchor it to commitment here.

steps.prompt: The charge nurse leans in. "Why the ED? Techs on the floors have easier nights."

choices.text: "Because I like helping people, and the ED helps the people who need it most."
choices.feedback: Every applicant says this. It is not wrong, it is invisible. Nothing in the answer proves you know what the department actually does.

choices.text: "Because ED patients come in undifferentiated, so the department has to rule out the thing that kills first, and the tech is the hands on almost every early step: the EKG, the blood, the vitals, the glucose. I want to be the part that makes the first ten minutes fast."
choices.feedback: This is the answer. It describes the work accurately, uses the department's own reasoning, and places you in it concretely. The panel now believes you know what you applied for.

choices.text: "I like the adrenaline. Trauma, codes, that kind of thing."
choices.feedback: Honest, and it worries experienced staff. Most of an ED shift is not adrenaline, and someone here for the codes tends to disengage during the other eleven hours.

choices.text: "The schedule works better for me, three twelves instead of five days."
choices.feedback: A real and legitimate reason, and a weak answer to this question. The panel asked about the work. Schedule preference belongs in the availability discussion.

steps.prompt: The educator: "Tell me about a time you dealt with somebody who was furious with you."

choices.text: "A customer screamed at me about a return policy. I stayed calm, explained the policy clearly, and eventually she accepted she was wrong and left."
choices.feedback: The structure is fine and the result is the problem. The outcome you named is being right. In the ED, the outcome that matters is that the person came down.

choices.text: "Saturday rush, a customer was shouting at the counter with a line behind him. I moved him to the end of the counter away from the audience, let him finish without interrupting, said back what I heard him say, told him what I could actually do and what I couldn't, and gave him two options. He picked one. He left calm, and no manager was involved. I did that twenty-some times a week."
choices.feedback: Situation, task, action, result, in the first person, with the scale attached. Every move in it is a real de-escalation technique: reduce the audience, listen without interrupting, reflect back, set honest limits, offer choices.

choices.text: "I got my manager, because that's what the policy said to do with escalated customers."
choices.feedback: Following policy is defensible, but the answer contains no action of your own. The question is asking what you personally do with an angry human being in front of you.

choices.text: "I don't really get rattled, so I've never had a situation like that turn into a problem."
choices.feedback: This reads as either no experience or no self-awareness, and it refuses the question. Panels ask behavioral questions to hear a story; declining to give one scores as a non-answer.

steps.prompt: The charge nurse: "It's 0300, I'm in a room with a sick patient, and I call out to you to push the antibiotic that's hanging in room 9. What do you do?"

choices.text: "I'd do it. You're the nurse, it's your order, and at 0300 you need the help."
choices.feedback: Instant fail. Medication administration is outside the tech scope no matter who asks and no matter how busy it is. Willingness to work outside your scope is the single most alarming thing a candidate can say in an ED interview.

choices.text: "I'd tell you that's not in my scope. Medications are a nursing task."
choices.feedback: Correct and incomplete. You have declined the task and left a busy nurse with the same problem she had ten seconds ago. Half the answer is missing.

choices.text: "I'd say I'm not able to give medications, ask what you need to happen for room 9, and then do whatever I can do, grab vitals, get the line flushed by someone who can, and find you another nurse to push it. Then I'd tell you when it was done."
choices.feedback: Three parts: decline the task, keep the relationship, solve her problem, and then close the loop. This is the answer the question is built to find.

choices.text: "I'd report the request, because asking a tech to give a medication is a safety issue."
choices.feedback: Escalating first to a report leaves the patient's antibiotic hanging and treats a hurried request as misconduct. Solve the clinical problem in the moment; patterns of unsafe requests get raised later, through the educator.

steps.prompt: The director: "This line is nights, every other weekend, and a holiday rotation. Is that going to work for you?" You can do it, and you also have an anatomy lab on Tuesday mornings.

choices.text: "Yes, nights and weekends work. I do have a Tuesday morning class this semester, so I'd want to avoid Monday nights if the schedule allows, but I can work around it either way."
choices.feedback: Clear yes first, one specific constraint second, flexibility third. Managers can build around a named constraint; they cannot build around vagueness, and they resent finding out in month two.

choices.text: "Yes, absolutely, anything works."
choices.feedback: Overcommitting feels strong and creates the first conflict in six weeks, which costs more credibility than the constraint ever would have. Say the true thing now.

choices.text: "Mostly. I'd have to see the schedule first before I could commit to weekends."
choices.feedback: Every hedge on availability costs you, because availability is what the department is actually buying. If the answer is yes, lead with yes.

choices.text: "Yes. Can I ask how the scheduling works, self-scheduling or blocks, and how far in advance it posts?"
choices.feedback: A clean yes plus a professional operational question. Not quite as strong as also naming the class constraint up front, but it answers the question and gathers something you need.

steps.prompt: "We're about at time. What questions do you have for us?"

choices.text: "How long is the precepted orientation, what does the tech actually do here in terms of draws and IVs, and what separates a tech who does well in this department from one who struggles? And what are the next steps and your timeline?"
choices.feedback: Four questions that all produce usable information, ending with the one that controls your follow-up. Ask the timeline question in every interview you ever have.

choices.text: "No, I think you covered everything. Thank you for your time."
choices.feedback: Scored as low interest almost universally. The closing question is part of the evaluation, not a courtesy, and silence here undoes a good hour.

choices.text: "What's the PTO policy, and how soon could I transfer to another department if I wanted to?"
choices.feedback: Both are legitimate questions and both are wrong now. The first reads as counting days off before day one; the second says you are already planning to leave the department you are interviewing for.

choices.text: "Does the system offer tuition reimbursement, and when does eligibility start?"
choices.feedback: A good question that employers expect and that signals long-term intent rather than disloyalty. It would be stronger paired with a question about the work itself.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern: a panel is not testing knowledge, it is testing three things. Do you know what this job actually is, will you stay inside your scope when someone senior pushes, and will the staff want to work next to you at 0300.

Every strong answer above had the same shape. It described the work in concrete terms, it used the first person, and it ended with an action or an outcome rather than an adjective. Every weak answer was either a feeling ('I like helping people'), a hedge ('mostly'), or a willingness to be useful past the line ('I'd do it, you're the nurse').

Two lines are worth memorizing exactly. For scope: I'm not able to do that, what do you need to happen, here's what I can do, and I'll find you someone who can. For closing: what are the next steps and when do you expect to decide.

Send the thank-you email within 24 hours to each of the three, three to five sentences, naming something specific one of them said. Then follow up once, three days past the timeline they gave. Then stop.

scenarios.title: First shift, four small tests
scenarios.intro:
Your third shift off orientation classroom work, first shift on the floor with a preceptor. 1900 to 0700, a 34-bed community ED, eleven boarders, a full waiting room by 2100.

Your competency checklist is signed for vital signs, point-of-care glucose, 12-lead EKG, specimen collection, transport, and safe patient handling. It is not signed for urinary catheters or splinting yet. You are not signed off for anything involving medications and never will be, because that is not a tech skill anywhere.

Four things happen tonight. None of them is a medical emergency. All four are the kind of moment that decides what people think of you by week three.

steps.prompt: 2140. A nurse you have not met calls from the doorway of room 14: "Hey, new guy, can you drop a Foley in 14 for me? I'm drowning." Catheters are not signed off on your checklist. Your preceptor is on break.

choices.text: Do it. You watched two of them in orientation, the nurse asked, and refusing on your first shift will make you look useless.
choices.feedback: This is the mistake that ends new techs. The checklist is the hospital's legal record of what you may do unsupervised; a nurse's permission does not substitute for it, and if the patient is injured you are performing a procedure you were never credentialed for.

choices.text: "I'm not signed off for Foleys yet. I can set the tray up, get her positioned, and stay to assist, and I'll grab someone who can place it. Want me to get vitals while I'm in there?"
choices.feedback: Correct on all three counts: you declined the task, you kept the relationship, and you solved her actual problem, which was time. Offering to assist also moves you toward getting signed off.

choices.text: "Sorry, that's not on my checklist." Then go back to your assignment.
choices.feedback: The decision is right and the delivery leaves a drowning nurse exactly where she was. In a department that runs on favors, the flat no is remembered longer than the reason for it.

choices.text: Text your preceptor on break to ask what to do.
choices.feedback: Not harmful, and it wastes the nurse's time on a question you can already answer: not signed off means not alone. Interrupting a break for a settled rule is also how you spend goodwill you will need later.

steps.prompt: 2320. Charting your rounds, you notice the vitals you took on room 7 at 2215 were entered under room 9. Room 9 is a chest pain patient whose real pulse was in the 40s; the numbers you accidentally posted there show a rate of 88 and look reassuring.

choices.text: Tell the nurse for room 9 immediately, say exactly what happened and when, then correct the record per policy and complete the safety report.
choices.feedback: Immediately is the operative word. A falsely reassuring heart rate on a chest pain patient can change a disposition decision. Speed of disclosure is the entire difference between an error and an incident.

choices.text: Fix the entry quietly. The correct numbers will be in there, and nobody needs a report over a data entry slip.
choices.feedback: Records are versioned and audited, so the change is visible and now looks like concealment. You have converted a routine error into the one category that ends employment.

choices.text: Re-take vitals on both patients right now so current numbers are in the chart, then tell the nurse what happened.
choices.feedback: Fresh vitals are genuinely useful and the instinct to make the patient safe first is right. But telling the nurse comes first here, because a bradycardic chest pain patient may need someone at the bedside before you finish a second set of vitals.

choices.text: Mention it at shift change so the oncoming tech knows to watch for it.
choices.feedback: That is a seven-hour delay on wrong-patient data in an active chart. Handoff is for continuing information, not for disclosing a safety problem that exists right now.

steps.prompt: 0110. Room 22's son steps into the hallway and blocks you: "Four hours. Four hours and nobody has done anything for my mother. What is wrong with you people?" He is loud enough that the hallway turns to look. He is not threatening anyone.

choices.text: "Sir, I understand, but everyone here is waiting and we're doing the best we can. Yelling in the hallway isn't going to speed anything up."
choices.feedback: Two errors in one sentence. 'I understand, but' erases everything before the but, and telling an angry person their behavior is counterproductive is heard as a challenge. This is how a loud man becomes a security call.

choices.text: Step slightly out of the hallway traffic, keep your hands visible, let him finish without interrupting, then: "Four hours is a long time and nobody has told you what's happening. I can't change how long the wait is. What I can do is tell your mom's nurse right now that you need an update, and get your mom a warm blanket and some water if she's allowed. Which of those first?"
choices.feedback: This is the whole toolkit in one move: reduce the audience, listen without interrupting, name the real grievance (information, not time), state honestly what you cannot do, then offer two concrete choices you can actually deliver.

choices.text: "Let me get the charge nurse for you." Walk away to find her.
choices.feedback: Getting the charge nurse is reasonable and the walking away is the problem. Leaving mid-sentence reads as dismissal and usually escalates, and he came to you. Acknowledge first, then bring the charge nurse into it.

choices.text: "The doctor will be in to see her shortly, I promise."
choices.feedback: Never promise a provider's arrival. You cannot control it, and when it does not happen the family stops believing anything anyone tells them for the rest of the visit, including things that matter.

steps.prompt: 0250. You bring a nurse a completed 12-lead. Without looking up she says, sharply, "Why is this taking so long? I asked for that twenty minutes ago." It actually took eleven minutes because the patient was in the bathroom. Two other staff are standing right there.

choices.text: "Patient was in the bathroom, I got it as soon as she was back. It's from 0246, rate looked around 110. Anything else you need in there?"
choices.feedback: Flat, factual, no defensiveness, and it ends with an offer. You gave the time, the finding, and moved on. This is exactly how you keep a bad hour from becoming a bad relationship.

choices.text: "It's been eleven minutes, not twenty. The patient was in the bathroom, which isn't my fault."
choices.feedback: You are right, and correcting her in front of two colleagues at 0250 wins the sentence and loses the shift. Save the correction; nothing about the patient's care depends on her having the exact number.

choices.text: Say nothing, set the EKG on the counter, and walk out.
choices.feedback: An EKG handed over without a time and without a word is a real clinical gap, not just a mood. It also leaves her believing the delay was what she thinks it was.

choices.text: "Sorry." Then go tell your preceptor how unfair that was.
choices.feedback: Apologizing for something that was not a failure teaches people to blame you, and taking it to the preceptor as a grievance on shift three makes the sharpness the story instead of the work. Nurses are short during bad hours and it is almost never about you.

steps.prompt: 0640. Twenty minutes to handoff. Your preceptor is finishing her charting and will sign your competency line for specimen collection. She asks, "So how'd it go?"

choices.text: "Good, no problems."
choices.feedback: There were four problems and you handled three of them. Saying nothing hides the wrong-patient vitals error from the person whose job is to teach you, and wastes the most useful twenty minutes of the night.

choices.text: "Mostly good. I put a set of vitals on the wrong patient at 2215, caught it at 2320, told the nurse and filed the report. What's one thing I should be doing differently?"
choices.feedback: Self-reports the error before she hears it elsewhere, states what was done about it, and then asks the single most valuable question a new employee can ask. Ask it again at 30 days.

choices.text: "Fine, except the nurse in zone 2 has a problem with me."
choices.feedback: On shift three you do not have enough information to conclude that, and opening with a personnel complaint frames you as someone who keeps score. If a pattern is real, it will still be real in a month.

choices.text: "Good. Can you sign off my specimen collection line, and what do I need to do to get signed off for Foleys and splinting?"
choices.feedback: Driving your own competency checklist forward is genuinely good practice and shows initiative. It would be stronger if you also disclosed the charting error, which she will see in the safety report anyway.

scenarios.debrief:
Four moments, one pattern: in every one, the right move had two halves. Decline or admit, then solve.

The Foley: not signed off means not alone, and the sentence that works is 'I can't do that, here's what I can do, and I'll find you someone who can.' A checklist signature is the hospital's legal record of your competence, and no verbal permission replaces it.

The wrong-patient vitals: speed of disclosure is everything. A falsely reassuring heart rate in a chest pain chart can change a disposition. Departments expect errors from new staff and have systems to catch them, and those systems only work if you speak within minutes, not at handoff.

The son in the hallway: he was not angry about four hours, he was angry about four hours of silence. Acknowledge, state honestly what you cannot control, then offer two things you can actually deliver. Never promise the provider is coming.

The sharp nurse: bad hours make people short, and almost none of it is about you. Answer with the fact and the time, offer the next thing, and let it go. Correcting a colleague in front of an audience costs more than being right is worth.

And the last one: ask for feedback out loud, early, and in one sentence. 'What is one thing I should be doing differently?' Ask it at the end of orientation and again at 30 days, then visibly do the thing.
